provenance.notes: Sign in with Google (OpenID Connect: the authorization address, the token endpoint, the userinfo), under the Google APIs Terms of Service (last modified 2021-11-09) and the Google API Services User Data Policy (last updated 2024-02-15). Limits: Google publishes no request figure for its OAuth and OpenID Connect endpoints, so they are unknown (null); the terms say Google sets and enforces limits and forbid circumventing them (section 2(d)). Omniauth guards no sign-in with a usage limit: one counted for the whole application would let anyone who exhausts it refuse every user's sign-in; a refused exchange (a 429 included) is a ProviderError and the sign-in is refused, never bypassed. Rights: commercial use is not restricted by the terms (no such clause; disruptive commercial messages and unlawful gambling are forbidden, 4(a)(5)); user data only to provide or improve user-facing features, never transferred or sold (User Data Policy: storage 'contract', redistribution 'forbidden'); content kept no longer than its cache headers allow (5(e)), no retention period beyond. A privacy policy that documents the use of the user data is required, its URL in the OAuth client's configuration. Branding: the button follows the Sign in with Google branding guidelines (https://developers.google.com/identity/branding-guidelines: 'Sign in with Google', 'Sign up with Google' or 'Continue with Google', the standard 'G' logo unchanged) - a display requirement, not a credit, hence no attribution. An External app in production that shows a logo or a name on the consent screen needs brand verification (https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/production-readiness/brand-verification); an unverified app has a user cap (no figure given there). The key is the OAuth client (client_id and client_secret).

No third party: the codes are computed and checked on the site's server (RFC 6238, over spomky-labs/otphp, MIT), the secrets sealed with the site's own sodium key; nothing is called, so there is no rate limit ([]) and no key of an account. The licence is the library's (MIT, its notice kept in vendor/ as Composer installs it). The tries a visitor may make are omniauth's Throttle ('totp': 5 every 15 minutes per account by default), an authentication rule of the site's, not a usage policy: this file limits nothing.

No third party: the passkeys are registered and checked on the site's server (WebAuthn, over web-auth/webauthn-lib, MIT) against the browser's authenticator; attestation 'none', so no metadata service (FIDO MDS) is fetched and nothing is called: no rate limit ([]), no key. The licence is the library's (MIT, its notice kept in vendor/ as Composer installs it). This file limits nothing; a sign-in's tries are omniauth's Throttle.

provenance.notes: Rate limits read 2026-11-10 on Bridge's API basics. Not declared, as the schema cannot count them exactly: 10 /authenticate requests per user a minute (an endpoint this package does not call), 4 Connect Sessions per item in 24 hours (counted per bank item, and connect()'s return leg sends nothing), 60 attachment downloads a minute (not used), and undisclosed limits on the endpoints without authentication. The limits count operations; one may be several requests (user creation, a new token, pages of transactions). Production access is under a contract with Perspecteev (Bridge's published conditions cover the sandbox, https://dashboard.bridgeapi.io/assets/pdf/cgu_EN.pdf, and the end users), hence the rights 'contract'. PSD2 (Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/389, the RTS on strong customer authentication and secure communication, Art. 36(5)(b), as amended by Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/2360, applicable since 2023-07-25, which changed Art. 10 and added Art. 10a, not Art. 36): an AISP accesses designated payment accounts 'where the payment service user does not actively request such information, no more than four times in a 24-hour period, unless a higher frequency is agreed' with the bank (text read 2026-11-10 at https://lawplayer.com/eu/act/32018R0389, EUR-Lex's own pages refusing automated reading; the EBA Q&A 2018_4210 counts four requests, each may carry balances and transactions). The Payment Services Regulation and PSD3 (final texts April 2026) were not yet in the Official Journal on 2026-11-10, so the RTS still applies. Bridge is the AISP and schedules the bank refreshes within it; omnibank's reads answer from Bridge's data and trigger no bank access. Writes: connect() creates a Bridge user (POST /v3/aggregation/users) the first time and a connect session each time; Bridge documents no idempotency key, so nothing is repeated - a failure after Bridge created the user leaves an unused Bridge user, and the caller's new connect() creates another.

No remote service: the statements are files the bank exported (CAMT.053, OFX, CSV) read from the connection's state, and a transfer is a pain.001 file written for the account holder to upload to the bank. No rate limit ([]), no key; what may be done with the files is the bank's contract with its customer. A transfer is never sent by this package: each transfer() writes a new file with a new message id, so a file written twice and uploaded twice is two payments - give each transfer its endToEndId and upload one file per transfer.

Powens is reached under a contract (its Terms and Conditions of Sale: a non-exclusive, non-transferable right to use the API; the end user accepts Powens' own Terms and Conditions of Use in the Webview, https://www.powens.com/sas-conditions-use/, which say the Partner has its own contract with Powens). Its fair usage policy (read 2026-11-10) publishes no production limit: only the sandbox's, 30 calls a minute and 86,400 a day for the 'Default' client type, so the limits are unknown here (null); a plan is tuned with Powens' key account manager. It advises webhooks over polling, and a manual refresh only when the end user asks, for one user. PSD2 (Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/389, the RTS on strong customer authentication and secure communication, Art. 36(5)(b), as amended by Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/2360, applicable since 2023-07-25, which changed Art. 10 and added Art. 10a, not Art. 36): an AISP accesses designated payment accounts 'where the payment service user does not actively request such information, no more than four times in a 24-hour period, unless a higher frequency is agreed' with the bank (text read 2026-11-10 at https://lawplayer.com/eu/act/32018R0389, EUR-Lex's own pages refusing automated reading; the EBA Q&A 2018_4210 counts four requests, each may carry balances and transactions). The Payment Services Regulation and PSD3 (final texts April 2026) were not yet in the Official Journal on 2026-11-10, so the RTS still applies. Powens is the AISP: it schedules the bank synchronisations within that rule; omnibank's reads (accounts, balances, transactions) answer from what Powens synced and trigger no bank access, so the rule is not a limit of this package. Writes: connect() creates a Powens user (POST /auth/init) the first time; Powens offers no idempotency key, so the package never repeats it - a failure after Powens created the user leaves an unused user, and the caller's new connect() creates another.

CalDAV is a protocol: each server's own terms and limits apply, and the site configures them (policy). Read on 2026-11-10: iCloud (https://caldav.icloud.com/, which answers from a pNN-caldav.icloud.com partition) needs an app-specific password, which needs two-factor authentication, at most 25 active, all revoked when the Apple Account password changes (https://support.apple.com/en-us/102654); Apple publishes no CalDAV developer terms nor limits. Fastmail (https://caldav.fastmail.com/) needs an app password, and its Basic plan has no CalDAV (https://www.fastmail.help/hc/en-us/articles/1500000278342); no limits documented. Nextcloud (https://<host>/remote.php/dav) throttles failed logins, no read limit documented. Google's CalDAV (https://apidata.googleusercontent.com/caldav/v2/) takes OAuth 2.0 only and shares the Calendar API's quotas (10,000 requests a minute per project, 600 a minute per user; https://developers.google.com/workspace/calendar/api/guides/quota): a site using it tightens this policy with them. The free-busy-query REPORT (RFC 4791 §7.10) is not supported by Google (its CalDAV guide) and reported unsupported by iCloud: busy time is then computed from the events of the span.

rateLimits.note: Calendar API: 10,000 requests a minute per Google Cloud project (sliding window), since 2026-05-01; projects that used the API between November 2025 and April 2026 keep their former quotas. Over it Google answers 403 or 429 (usageLimits: rateLimitExceeded).
600 requests a minute per user per project (sliding window): 403 userRateLimitExceeded over it. Count it per user: Registry::calendarEvents($name, $user).
1,000,000 requests a day per project is the threshold before charges apply and cannot be raised; Google announced charges beyond it for later in 2026, with 90 days' notice at least.

provenance.notes: Commercial use is not forbidden by the Google APIs Terms of Service; no sublicensing, no substitute for the API, no circumventing the limits. Caching is left unknown: the terms forbid keeping API content beyond what its cache headers allow (§5(e)), while a user's own events are user data under the Google API Services User Data Policy, which sets no time to live. Storage is allowed for the user-facing feature the user consented to, under Limited Use (https://developers.google.com/terms/api-services-user-data-policy): secured in transit and at rest, no transfer but the listed exceptions, no human reading without the user's agreement, no ads; deleted when the terms end (§8(b)). Redistribution is forbidden (no sublicensing, no transfer of user data). No attribution is required; the branding rules apply: say "for" or "compatible with" Google Calendar with a trademark notice, never use the mark as the site's name or logo. Calendar scopes are sensitive: an external app needs Google's verification (a privacy policy, a home page, a verified domain, a justification per scope, a demo video); an unverified app is capped at 100 new users, and an app in Testing status gets refresh tokens that last 7 days. A refresh token also dies unused for 6 months, when the user revokes access, or past 100 per account per client.

provenance.notes: Microsoft APIs Terms of Use (last updated October 2025): a limited, revocable licence for applications offered to customers, no ban on commercial use (Microsoft may set fees or limits at any time). Caching and storage are marked allowed under those conditions. Permissions: Calendars.Read to read, Calendars.ReadWrite to write, offline_access for a refresh token; getSchedule's pages disagree (Calendars.ReadBasic in the reference, Calendars.Read in the concept page): Calendars.Read holds under both. getSchedule is for work or school accounts only, not personal Microsoft accounts.

A PutObject, a DeleteObject and a CopyObject of the same key are idempotent: a replay leaves the same object. A multipart upload's CreateMultipartUpload replayed leaves an incomplete upload that is never completed (it costs storage until aborted: give the bucket an AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload lifecycle rule), never a second object; an UploadPart replayed replaces the same part.

Shopify's real rule for the Admin GraphQL API is cost-based: a leaky bucket of query cost points restored at 100 points a second on the standard plans (200 Advanced, 1,000 Plus, 2,000 Commerce Components), each query at most 1,000 points, the bucket's state in every answer (extensions.cost.throttleStatus), which the provider's client reads and waits on. Two requests a second is the REST Admin API's leak rate on the standard plans.

provenance.notes: Limits per app and store. Not expressible in the schema: cost points per query (computed by Shopify per query and plan). Per store with 500,000 variants or more, 10,000 new variants a day (outside Shopify Plus); input arrays of 250 items at most; pagination up to 25,000 objects. Shopify documents no idempotency for draftOrderCreate: the provider never retries a mutation.

rateLimits.note: Stripe's global limit in a sandbox, and the default limit of each endpoint in both modes; live mode's global limit is 100 a second. One policy for both modes: the stricter is declared.
Connect account creations in a sandbox; 30 a second in live mode.

provenance.notes: Limits per account, per mode (docs.stripe.com/rate-limits, read 2026-11-10): global 100 requests a second live, 25 in a sandbox; 25 a second per endpoint unless noted; 1,000 updates an hour per PaymentIntent; Files 20 reads and 20 writes a second; Search 20 reads a second; Payouts 15 creations a second; Connect account creations 30 a second live, 5 in a sandbox; subscriptions 10 new invoices a minute and 20 a day each. Concurrency: 50 requests in flight in live mode by default, not published for sandboxes (not declared). Reads: on average no more than 500 per transaction over 30 days, at least 10,000 a month (not expressible: it depends on the transactions). A 429 carries Stripe-Rate-Limited-Reason; a 429 lock_timeout is not processed either. Writes carry the caller's Idempotency-Key. Use is governed by the Stripe Services Agreement (commercial, storage, redistribution: the contract's).

The REST API (wc/v3) sets no rate limit of its own: the shop is the merchant's own WordPress, and its host (a firewall, a security plugin, the hosting company) may limit it - a site adds that as its own tightening. WooCommerce's Store API rate limiting is opt-in and applies to the Store API only, which this provider does not call. The shop's data is the merchant's: redistribution depends on them.

Per feed: each network publishes its GTFS and GTFS-Realtime under its own licence and terms, so a feed's policy is the site's to give where it configures the feed - its licence (option licence: "ODbL-1.0", "etalab-2.0") and the credit its licence asks (option attribution), shown by Capabilities and Registry::policy(); a tightening (option policy: a GTFS-Realtime feed's rate limit, the licence's rights) on top. The static feed is read from the site's own store: no call is counted. A GTFS-Realtime feed's limits are its publisher's, unknown here.
